newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: IVORY COAST DONORS FOCUS ON ROLE OF CAISTAB.
newsitem.headline: IVORY COAST DONORS FOCUS ON ROLE OF CAISTAB.

text.p: Ivorian commodities reform talks with donors get under way on Tuesday as part of discussions on a three-year economic policy blueprint and an Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility from the IMF.
"Tomorrow we will meet the Caistab (state commodities marketing board) and the Minister of Agriculture," a donor delegate said, adding that decisions were unlikely before next Monday.

Caistab reforms might include privatisation. "It is a possibility," he said, referring to the former state monopoly which until 1995/96 controlled almost all points of internal and external marketing of coffee and cocoa.

Ivorian Agriculture Minister Lambert Kouassi Konan said in a recent interview with a Paris-based magazine there was "no taboo" against privatising the Caistab, whose officials have fiercely resisted such a move.
Ivory Coast has loosened controls on cocoa and coffee marketing under the terms of a $150 million agriculture credit from the World Bank, which wants further changes.
Ivory Coast in 1996 agreed to sweeping coffee marketing reforms from 1998/99 and to more changes for cocoa from 1999/2000, but full details have yet to be decided and officially announced.
Donors want the state Caistab to hand farm-to-port price-setting to the private sector, with exporters possibly playing a role in export contract auction management.
"The talks deal with reforms from 1998/99, not for the next season (1997/98)," said the delegate.
World Bank officials see privatisation as a way to raise prices paid to farmers in the longer term.
The Caistab was set up by founding President Felix Houphouet-Boigny as a means of controlling exports and revenue.
It guarantees exporters a minimum price, making payments to them when necessary and taking back surpluses when export prices rise above the level set.
Caistab advocates say the Board irons out world price swings caused by what they see as rampant speculation by London and New York commodities futures traders.
It also guarantees crop quality, they say, although up-country checking stations were closed in 1995/96 in favour of Caistab-approved and port-based private quality checkers.
Complaints over quality are still voiced by industry buyers.

Critics say funds from surplus years continue to be transferred to the treasury for use in the wider economy, despite debts to some exporters which arose when cocoa and coffee prices slipped from 1986 onwards.
They also say arbitrary marketing decisions by the Caistab have cost Ivory Coast money, and that current farmgate prices for cocoa of 500 CFA a kilo are unattractive.
In 1988/89, Houphouet-Boigny challenged the world market price after falls by taking the season's crop off the market.
Other producers such as Cameroon have already dismantled state commodities boards, with varying degrees of success.
Industry analysts see a decision by Ivory Coast in July to transfer management of Caistab funds to the treasury from a state bank as a first step to potentially wider reforms.
